1:
Jericho is remarked on before its citizen. Henry notes the city was built under a curse and yet honoured with Christ's presence, the gospel taking away the curse, though it was no sin to live there once it stood; Gill observes he passed straight through, having no work there. On the name they agree: Zacchaeus is the Hebrew Zaccai, meaning pure, so the man was a Jew, though Clarke adds his trade made his countrymen treat him as a heathen. Lightfoot examines and rejects the identification with the Zaccai who fathered Rabban Jochanan — a Rabbin's degree is hardly credible in a publican, and that Zaccai was of priestly descent, so a priest and a publican would have seemed a monster among them.

The office itself is reconstructed with some care. Robertson notes the word for chief publican occurs nowhere else, its sense plain from parallel compounds, and makes him head of collections for a region trading in balsam. Ellicott fills in the economics: Jericho stood near the fords and drew the balsam of Gilead, its dates and palm-honey probably paying duty, so the Roman farming system left Zacchaeus a middle-man between the real capitalists of the equestrian order and the men who actually collected, with as many opportunities of enriching himself as a Turkish pacha. Wesley calls it drily a very honourable and profitable place. Barnes thinks the wealth recorded because it was so unlikely a rich man should follow one so despised.

What he was seeking divides them. Barnes and Clarke say plainly it was curiosity, Barnes drawing the lesson that God uses every principle — curiosity, sympathy, affection, hope, fear — to bring men into the way of salvation. Ellicott resists: the motive is left to be inferred, and mere curiosity would not have won the Lord's warm approval, so he asks whether the man had heard that a publican was among the chosen disciples, or been stirred by the miracle at the town's entrance. Titus Bostrensis takes the highest view, that the seed of salvation had begun to spring in him, since no one who truly sees Jesus can remain in wickedness. Henry stands between, granting the curiosity and turning it forward — the eye is not satisfied with seeing, and we should seek to see Jesus with an eye of faith.

The obstacles are read literally, then figuratively. Titus Bostrensis names two, the crowd and the man's smallness, and says the multitude that hindered him was not so much of men as of his sins; Ambrose asks why the Evangelist describes this man's stature and no one else's, and suggests he was young in wickedness or still weak in faith, since one who could climb was not yet prostrate in sin. Henry finds the reason on the other side, that Christ did not study to show himself and was not carried on men's shoulders as a pope in procession, neither he nor his kingdom coming with observation, so he was simply lost in a crowd on a day of humiliation.

The tree draws both the botanist and the allegorist. Ellicott distinguishes three trees that have borne the name and settles on the fig-mulberry, which grew tall in the Jordan valley, remarking that Luke's care to keep it distinct from the sycamine of an earlier chapter is the botanical accuracy one expects of a physician. Clarke turns the defect into an advantage — had he been as tall as the rest he might have passed unnoticed, and even the imperfections of our persons may be made subservient to grace. Henry sees him forget the gravity of his office and run ahead like a boy, Wesley that desire conquered honour and shame. Bede reads the name the Latins gave it, the foolish fig, and makes it the Cross, which sustains believers as the fig sustains its fruit and is mocked by unbelievers as foolishness.
5:
The invitation came from the guest, and that strikes them first. Ambrose says he invites himself uninvited, seeing the will before he heard the word; Calvin calls it a remarkable favour that the Lord anticipates the man and asks lodging of his own accord, though it was a greater gift to dwell in his heart than to enter his house. Barnes makes it one among a thousand instances where the Saviour goes beyond the desert, desire and expectation of men, and notes he does not disdain the mansions of the rich, provided there be a humble heart. Ellicott adds local detail: Jericho was then a city of the priests, so the Lord passed over their houses to lodge with a publican. Robertson renders the command bluntly — come down in a hurry.

The murmuring is examined for its extent. Ellicott notes it was not confined to rigorous Pharisees but came from the whole crowd, the chief publican being plainly unpopular and the town's priestly character strengthening every caste feeling; Robertson hears in the compound verb something onomatopoetic, like the cooing of doves or the hum of bees, and observes that Jesus had been the hero of this Galilean crowd until he shocked it. Wesley alone softens it: most murmured from surprise, not indignation. Calvin turns it on the murmurers: the world disregards the offer of God's grace and yet complains bitterly when it is carried to others; and he insists the word sinner here does not mean what we ordinarily call one, since collecting taxes was no crime in itself.

The restitution is measured against the law. Lightfoot supplies the rabbinic frame: ill-gotten goods had to be distributed among the poor by a set form of words, while alms from honest wealth were capped at a fifth, as decreed at Usha — so Zacchaeus went far beyond the rule, his fourfold restitution matching the law of theft. Pseudo-Chrysostom presses that he does not wait for the judgment of the law but makes himself his own judge, and infers his estate cannot have been wholly unjust gains, else he could not restore fourfold from the remainder. Theophylact reckons nothing was left of his own, half going to the poor and the fourfold out of the remainder, and marks the tense — not I will give, but I give. Henry hears the same, a present deed and not a bequest, and guesses he had heard how the rich young ruler broke with Christ over such a command, and resolved otherwise.

The verdict on the house is a verdict on the man. Theophylact says the house means the man who lives in it, since the name son of Abraham would not be given to a lifeless building, and notes Christ says not that he was such a son but that he now is, having borne no likeness to Abraham while chief of the publicans. Bede grounds the title in imitation rather than descent — as Abraham left his country, so this man abandoned his goods by giving them away — and finds in the word also a declaration that not only those who have lived justly but those raised out of injustice belong to the sons of promise.

The closing sentence defends the whole scene. Pseudo-Chrysostom puts it in Christ's mouth: why accuse me if I bring sinners to righteousness, when so far am I from hating them that I came for their sakes? I came to heal and not to judge, and am the constant guest of the sick. He meets the obvious objection, that Paul forbids us to eat with a covetous brother — these were not yet so far advanced as to be brethren, and Paul's rule touches only those who persist, while these were converted. Cyril of Alexandria says the same of the calling: Christ calls near those afar off and gives light to those in darkness.
11:
The parable is given a reason before a meaning. Eusebius says some expected the kingdom to begin at the first coming, being astonished by the miracles, so Christ tells them he would not receive it until he had gone to his Father. Theophylact adds that in answering he showed himself God, knowing their thoughts. Calvin puts it severely: the disciples were aiming at the shadow of a kingdom, and by removing the expectation of an immediate reign he exhorts them to patience, since they must endure many toils before the glory for which they pant too earnestly.

The setting turns out to be recent politics. Barnes explains that Judea had been subject to Rome since Pompey and was governed by Jews holding office under the Romans, so a prince had to go to Rome to have his title recognised, as Archelaus and Antipas did before Augustus; Robertson observes it had happened while Jesus was a boy in Nazareth and was common knowledge. Clarke draws out the structure: the parable carries two distinct morals, the citizens' rejection and its punishment in the destruction of their state, which alone answers the words about the kingdom appearing immediately, and the servants' reward, which is all that Matthew's talents intend.

That difference from Matthew is worked carefully. Chrysostom sets the two side by side: in Luke different sums come out of the same principal, one servant bringing five and another ten from a single pound, whereas in Matthew the man with two adds two and the man with five gains as much again, so the rewards differ too. Ellicott draws the consequence, that here we begin with equality where Matthew begins with unequal amounts according to several ability, so the trust here is what all disciples hold in common — knowledge of the truth and membership in the kingdom — and not offices varying in degree. Bede says the same, one pound to each because there is one doctrine, one faith, one baptism; and Clarke protests that rendering the mina as a pound is an impropriety any reader can see.

Whether the number ten means anything divides them. Chrysostom takes it for a sign of perfection, since whoever counts beyond it must begin again from unity, having reached a goal at ten; Augustine reads the ten pounds as the law because of the commandments, and the ten servants as those to whom grace was preached while under it. Against them Barnes says nothing in particular is denoted, the number being a circumstance to keep the narrative going, and Gill that it is a round number for an uncertain one, the apostles being twelve and never called the ten — adding that the servants are not all mankind nor the elect, but the ministers of the gospel, since one of the ten proved wicked.

The commission and the rebellion are read together. Robertson notes the Greek says while I am coming rather than till I come, its verb appearing nowhere else in the New Testament; Ellicott explains that occupy is the older English for trading, as in Ezekiel. On the far country, Cyril and Theophylact take the journey for the ascension and the return for the second appearing, Cyril observing that Christ calls himself first a man, then noble, but not yet a king, since at his first appearing he exercised no kingly power. Calvin will have none of the subtleties: the phrase expresses nothing but a long absence running from his death to his last coming, for he reigns now in regenerating his people, but because that way of reigning is hidden from the flesh his manifestation is said to be delayed. Eusebius and Cyril agree the hostile citizens are the Jews, who rejected his kingdom by telling Pilate they had no king but Caesar; Augustine adds that the message sent after him continued past the resurrection, when they persecuted the apostles.
16:
The two faithful servants are identified before rewarded. Bede makes the first the order of teachers sent to the circumcision, whose single pound gained ten by uniting to itself the people under the law, and the second those sent to the uncircumcision, whose pound gained five by converting nations enslaved to the five bodily senses. On the cities Ambrose takes them for souls, over whom he is rightly set who has deposited his Lord's money in men's minds, as Jerusalem is called a city and so are peace-making souls. Ellicott presses that authority over ten cities must answer to some real energy and guidance in the unseen world and cannot be reduced to the beatific vision, while Barnes warns it is not to be looked for literally, the reward being simply proportioned to faithfulness.

The scale of the increase is noticed. Ellicott observes that where Matthew's servants merely double, these gain tenfold, and compares the thirty, sixty and hundredfold of the sower; Clarke makes the same distinction, the mina pointing to the gospel given alike to all who hear it and the talents to differing capacities for improving it. Chrysostom draws the contrast that carries the whole: in earthly wealth no man is made rich without another being made poor, but in spiritual riches none is enriched without enriching another.

The napkin is examined closely. Theophylact notes that a napkin covers the face of the dead, so the idler is well said to have wrapped his pound in one, leaving it dead and unprofitable; Robertson identifies the word as a Latin sweat-cloth transliterated into Greek, found in papyrus marriage contracts as part of a dowry; Ellicott adds that such cloths served then as now for concealing money a man wished to hoard. Augustine gives it a sharper application, to those who flatter themselves that each need answer only for himself, so that none need preach at all. Barnes states it plainly: men have talents, learning, property and influence, and keep them, and it would be the same for the world if God had never conferred them.

The excuse is turned into the sentence. Robertson traces austere to a verb meaning to dry up, rough to the taste and then harsh in disposition, and thinks the phrase about taking up what one laid not down a proverb for a grasping profiteer; Ellicott finds the same hardness, the word rendered churlish elsewhere. Barnes says the whole speech shows the sinner's view of God as unjust and demanding more than men can render — whereas the lesson is that since men know God will be just, they ought to be ready. Bede answers the servant on his own ground: if you knew me hard, why did that thought not strike you with terror? Ellicott notes the very term the servant dared to use is repeated back with solemn impressiveness, his words turned to his own condemnation.

The bank draws both the lexicographer and the allegorist. Robertson insists the increase demanded is proper legal interest and not usury; Wesley agrees that interest appears contrary to no law of God or man, but that this is no plea for such interest as implies oppression or extortion. Bede makes the money the preaching of the gospel, to be put out into hearts ready to receive it, and Augustine takes the bank for the public profession of religion itself. When the bystanders object, Robertson suspects a real interruption by an audience following the story keenly, Wesley hears admiration rather than envy, and Clarke reports the verse missing from Codex Bezae and some copies of the Itala. On the enemies, Theophylact says they were slain even in this world by the Roman army; Augustine turns the sentence against the Marcionites, who allow Christ to be good and call the God of the Old Testament evil, when here the Son does what they impute to the Father alone.
28:
The journey up is deliberate. Titus Bostrensis says those who saw him going to Jerusalem thought he meant to begin the kingdom there, and only after the parable had corrected the error did he go forward to his passion. Henry finds him foremost of the company, going forward bound in the spirit and knowing what awaited him, and asks whether we shall draw back from any service when he was so forward to die for us.

The two villages are given both a geography and an etymology. Bede places Bethphage on Mount Olivet as a village of the priests, with Bethany some fifteen stades from Jerusalem; Origen reads Bethany as the house of obedience and Bethphage as the house of cheek-bones, a priestly name because the cheek-bones of a sacrifice fell to the priests by law. Chrysostom notices a change of manner: at first he bore himself as indifferent to the Jews, but having proved his power he now transacts everything with the highest authority, foretelling the unbroken colt and that nobody would hinder them.

The colt concentrates the allegory. Ambrose finds it tied and unable to be loosed except at the Lord's command, so the apostle's hand looses it — be such, he says, that you may be able to loose those who are bound. He takes the colt for the Gentile people, on whom no man had sat because none before Christ called the nations into the Church; and he sets the two masteries against each other, that others bind in order to possess while Christ looses in order to keep, knowing that gifts are stronger than chains. Origen presses the same, that the colt had many masters until the Saviour had need of him and then had no other, since no one can serve God and mammon. Augustine settles the discrepancy between the Gospels shortly: where both an ass and a colt may be conceived there is no variance if one relates the one and another both.

The garments carry their own lesson. The Gloss notes the disciples served him not only with another man's colt but with their own clothes, and Bede that the other Evangelists have much of the crowd doing likewise; Henry observes drily that many will attend Christ at other people's expense who care to be at no charge upon him themselves. Ambrose gives the sitting an inward sense: the mystical Ruler takes his seat in the secret depths of men's souls, guiding the footsteps of the mind and bridling the wantonness of the heart, his word at once a rein and a goad.

At the descent the shout begins. Ellicott notes the Greek word for descent occurs in no other New Testament writer, a technical geographical term natural to one who may have studied Strabo; Robertson places them on the southern slope where the city bursts suddenly into view, and hears enthusiasm pent up since the parable and restrained no longer. Ellicott finds it characteristic of the Gentile Evangelist that glory replaces the Hosanna of the others, and that the multitude, prophesying unconsciously, say peace in heaven where the angels had said peace on earth; Henry sets the two songs side by side, the angels rejoicing in what men gain by Christ and the saints in what the angels gain. Wesley thinks they spoke from a divine impulse words most of them did not understand. When the Pharisees object, Ellicott takes them for the party that had granted him respect as a Teacher and could see nothing but frenzy in calling him king, Robertson for half-hearted followers inside the procession. Barnes reads the answer as proverbial, not meaning stones would be made conscious but that such joy could not properly be restrained; Henry claims a literal fulfilment, when men reviled Christ on the cross, his disciples fell silent, and the earth quaked and the rocks rent.
41:
The tears are read first as evidence. Origen observes that Christ confirms his own beatitudes by example, having said blessed are the meek and then learn of me for I am meek, and blessed are they that weep and then wept over the city; Cyril takes the tears for the token of a real humanity, without which his compassion would not have been plain to us. Henry notes that we never read he laughed but often find him in tears, that in this very place David had wept and the men of war with him, and that he wept in the midst of his triumph while all about him rejoiced.

Whose Jerusalem is wept over then gets extended. Cyril will not deny that the old city fell for the wickedness of its inhabitants, but asks whether the weeping may not also concern the spiritual Jerusalem, since a man who sins after receiving the mysteries of truth is wept over, and no Gentile is wept over but only one who was of Jerusalem and has ceased to be. Gregory says the Redeemer does not cease to weep through his elect whenever he sees any turn from a good life, and describes the corrupt soul as having its day, to which present things are peace because it shuns the foresight of a future that might disturb its mirth.

The sentence itself is broken, and they say so. Ellicott finds in the repeated pronoun the strongest possible emotion, and in the unfinished clause the deepest human sorrow the Son of Man had known, noting that the tense with now implies a concealment already completed. Robertson names the figure aposiopesis, the conclusion never expressed, the sudden break most impressive. Calvin says the discourse is pathetic and therefore abrupt, since men under vehement passion never more than half express their feelings, and hears two things mingled, a lament for the city and a reproach to an ungrateful people; on even thou he takes Christ to be contrasting Jerusalem with every other city, as a heavenly sanctuary set on earth. He draws the rule that men deserve heavier punishment in proportion to the gifts received, and that the nearer God comes with sound doctrine the less excusable is contempt of it.

The siege is described in words the commentators find remarkable. Ellicott notes a cluster of terms peculiar to Luke and belonging to the higher forms of historical composition, and explains that the noun means first a stake, then the stockade defending a besieger's camp, then the earthwork it stood on — the embankment rather than the excavation. On the fulfilment Wesley says simply that Titus performed it exactly, and Gregory that the overthrow was that of Vespasian and Titus, whose course we may gather from Josephus — a Jew who related each event in exact accordance with Christ's prophecies.

The charge at the end is the visitation refused. Theophylact glosses it as Christ's own coming, and says that had they believed they might have been reconciled to the Romans and exempted from danger, as those who believed were; Eusebius adds that his coming was to bring peace to those near and afar off, and that because they would not receive it, it was hidden from them. Lightfoot sets beside this what the rabbis made of the same ruin, one holding the city was destroyed for nothing but profanation of the sabbath, another for nothing but neglect of the phylacteries. Gregory turns the visitation inward: God ceases not to visit the wicked soul with teaching, by a scourge or by a miracle, but a soul that knows not the time is given over at the last to its enemies. Henry states the doctrine plainly: there is a time of visitation in which the things belonging to our peace may be known to good purpose, and none are so blind as those who will not see.
45:
The order of events is made to carry a charge. Gregory notes that having foretold the city's ruin he went straight into the temple to eject the traders, which shows the people's destruction arose chiefly from the guilt of the priests; Ambrose adds that God will not have his temple a house of traffic but a dwelling-place of holiness, nor the priestly service a saleable performance of religion rather than a free obedience. Gregory marks the sequel: having maintained discipline by the ejection, he pours out the gifts of grace by teaching daily. Cyril explains what was sold: animals for the sacrifices, by the custom of the law, at a time when the shadows were passing and the truth of Christ shining, so he reformed the customs and left the house a house of prayer. Theophylact recalls that he had done as much at the outset of his preaching, and did it again because the crime had grown by their not being chastened.

The traders are then turned into churchmen. Origen puts the sharpest form: if any man sells, let him be cast out, especially if he sells doves, for if I sell what the Holy Spirit has revealed to me, or will not teach without a fee, what do I but sell a dove? Ambrose drives out the money-changers as those who seek gain from the Lord's money, meaning the divine Scripture. Gregory presses further, that corrupt men in religious office make the house a den of thieves by slaying with the sword of their wickedness the neighbours they ought to have raised by their prayers; and he defines the two trades — the sellers part at a price with what is another's by right, since to sell justice is to keep it only for a reward, and the buyers, unwilling to do what is just, purchase sin by paying their patrons.

The temple itself is read figuratively. Augustine takes it for Christ in his human nature, and then for the Church joined to him, so that as head he could say destroy this temple, while as the body he says take these things hence — signifying men in the Church who pursue their own interest, or shelter there to conceal their wickedness, rather than follow the love of Christ.

The plot is given its occasion. Cyril says that after all he had done and said men ought to have worshipped him as God, and that so far from it they sought to kill him; Bede offers three grounds — that he taught daily, that he had cast out the thieves, or that he had come as King and Lord and been greeted with a heavenly hymn. Robertson notices that the first men of the people stand after the verb and apart from the chief priests and scribes, calling attention to them as a distinct group, and that the raising of Lazarus had brought the leaders of Jerusalem together for his destruction; Ellicott identifies them as notables of the city, whether of the Sanhedrin or not.

Why nothing came of it is answered two ways. Bede gives both: either they feared a tumult and knew not what to do with a man they had settled to destroy, or they sought his death precisely because they saw their authority set aside and the crowds flocking to hear him. Calvin draws from the same verse a description of the Church, which consisted of the despised multitude while its enemies were the guardians of religion — part of the folly of the cross, that God passes by the excellence of the world and chooses what is foolish and weak. He adds that even with good ground for pursuing Christ they had no right to proceed to murder after the manner of robbers, and that the conspiracy was frustrated because by God's secret purpose he was appointed to the death of the cross.
